newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DTB exchange to launch 2-yr futures.
newsitem.headline: German DTB exchange to launch 2-yr futures.

text.p: The German DTB futures and options exchange plans to introduce a futures contract on two-year debt in the first quarter of 1997, German stock exchange holding company Deutsche Boerse said on Tuesday.

The basket of paper deliverable into the futures contract will comprise of Treasury notes and longer-dated government debt with remaining maturities of one-and-three-quarter years to two-and-one-quarter years, Deutsche Boerse said in a statement.

The introduction will meet a demand for a hedging instrument covering the two-year segment of the yield curve and thereby, strengthen the German financial market in the run-up to European monetary union, the bourse said.
It added that after the new future was launched, the DTB would be the only exchange to offer mark-denominated futures contracts for the full maturity spectrum covering one month to 10-year paper.
The DTB launched a new one-month future last month and a new three-month Euromark contract is due for launch on January 14.
The two-year contract, to be launched as soon as possible in the first quarter of 1997, will be similar in structure to the DTB's existing five-year and 10-year futures contracts, the statement said.
It will have sufficient underlying volume due in part to the government's decision this year to start regular issues of two-year Treasury notes, the statement said.

The German government this year won the grudging approval of the Bundesbank to issue short-term government debt to help its bond market, the world's third largest, catch up with stiff international competition.
Bonn now issues six-month Treasury Bills, or Bubills, and two-year Treasury notes on a regular basis. The move is designed to plug gaping holes in a market dominated by five-year and 10-year issues.
Bonn for the first time issued 10 billion marks worth of two-year notes on September 18 and has set a further tender for December 17 for an issue expected to total up to eight billion marks.
